Dear dads,

I'm an adult daughter of a wonderful father. I didn't always think he was wonderful, however.

I always had my dad in my life, but I used to wish that wasn't the case. My dad had anger issues that began pretty early in my life. My dad is a big, tall, strong man. He can be physically intimidating. I was a headstrong little girl, too smart for my own good, and like any child I wanted my own way. When my dad started to feel frustrated and overwhelmed at his job, things began to go downhill.

He took his rage over the office home sometimes. I used to feel a sick feeling in my stomach when I would hear his car in this distance. He drove a mustang with a souped up engine and I could hear it a good distance from the house. I'd go run and hide in my room when he came home because I couldn't bear to see the scowl on his face.

My dad would often fly off the handle about what I thought were small things. I wasn't a neat child and I didn't clean my room as I was told. One time he entered it and found me sitting in my room when I was supposed to be cleaning it, playing with some toy, and he went ballistic. He forcibly threw me on the bed and started whacking me with his belt (now he'd always been a spanker, but this time wasn't like that--this time he was just venting anger, not disciplining me) over and over until I screamed. I'm telling you this not to make him seem like a bad person, but to illustrate the kinds of things he did that caused this rift between us. Once I left a towel lying on the livingroom floor in front of the television. He'd repeatedly told me to pick up after myself. I always had to be told things a million times. He grabbed a rubber thong and grabbed me and smacked my ass with it. The next day I had a shoe shaped bruise on my 9 year old butt that was beginning to darken to purple.

When I became a teenager and was not so easily cowed, you can't imagine the shouting matches we had. I used to run away from home in the dark of the night and go walking the streets by myself to get away when the fighting became too much. The day of my high school graduation we had a fight so outrageous that I jumped in my car to get away from him and he tried to block me from leaving the driveway. I was so scared and disoriented I ended up driving aimlessly for an hour and getting myself seriously lost. Hahahaha.. I eventually found my way back (this is before everyone had cell phones mind you, it was 1999, so I couldn't call anyone for help) but then I ended up locking the keys in my car. I won't tell the whole story because it is so long, but I barely made it to my own graduation and even when I did I was miserable and subdued and drained. I later found out my dad jumped in the car and was looking desperately for me. When he did find me he grabbed me and held me close. I remember dissolving into a pile of tears, so deep was my relief that my ordeal that day was over. I didn't even have the energy to hate him, even though I still blamed him for everything.

When I was in my 20s things had started to calm down. I was becoming older, and so was he. However, I do remember one horrible fight that ended in the back yard. I'd run away from his yelling, hulking form, slamming doors behind me, and he followed. And suddenly he just....stopped. And started sobbing. He began to tell me things, things I didn't want to know, things that didn't feel like my business.

He told me he'd thought of leaving my mother. My mom had been suffering from depression for years and stopped being involved in the marriage. I didn't see them argue much. His love for her was so deep, I don't think he knew what to do. I think he felt like a single father most of the time. Work was so* stressful* for him. He made good money doing what he was doing in mid-level management at a large corporation and he didn't want to take a demotion because it would have changed our living situation. He said sometimes he regretted not doing that, because what was the point of living in a nice house if the family was so miserable? (I have to agree) Everybody at work came to him to vent, expected miracles from him, took advantage of him. I now go through this same thing at my job. I'm Miss Fix-It. I'm the person people go to and they don't care that I have my own demanding job to go to. But unlike my dad, my income isn't dependent on my performance because I work for a government agency. I know the frustration this can cause--being a dependable, helpful, and capable person often means you're a target for abuse.

All these revelations didn't immediately fix our relationship, but that was the start of me seeing him in a different light. Instead of just dad, now he was a person, with his own identity and his own human feelings. I still had a LOT of rage towards him and my own personal demons to work through. It would be about ten years before I would have that "come to Jesus" moment that became my pivot in the change in our relationship. During those ten years my dad was changing and working on himself to become a better person. He prayed for the strength to calm himself down, to let little things go, to not respond to incorrect behavior from his family members in such a volatile way..and that had ripple effects. My mom began to heal from her depression. The change in him spurred her to look within herself and realize that she could not use her mood disorder as an excuse to withdraw from the family. This healed their relationship which in turn made my dad not just work to feel better but actually feel better!

Fast forward to now. I no longer have a love/hate relationship with my dad. I simply love my dad. Why? I forgave my dad. A lot of people feel unable to do this. You see, forgiveness is a commandment from God. And the devil tells you "why should you forgive that person? Look what they did to you, they don't deserve it" But what you don't realize is that forgiving people that hurt you promotes SELF HEALING. It's what lets you transform. It's what allows you to let go of the pain.

When I think about all this stuff now, I no longer just see what dad did to hurt me. I see the bigger picture. I see an overburdened man who had lost control of his family and was frantically trying to get it back. I see my OWN sins. I see my hypocrisy. I see my mother's failure to pull her weight, and her selfishness. I see my failure as a big sister. And I see a man who turned to God for help and was able to heal his family and win it back. And I wouldn't be seeing any of that if I hadn't made the decision to "try and forgive".

My dad is now my favorite person on this earth. He's my hero. He's my friend. The saddest I get now is thinking about how he's getting older, and someday he won't be with me. I want to marry a man like my dad. I think that's why I'm still single, to be honest with you. I can't find one like him, lol.

Father's day is coming up. There are so many people with dads who have failed them in deep, significant ways. There are people whose dads weren't involved in their lives. There are people whose dads went to prison. There are people whose dads did worse things than mine, by a long shot.

My point is that if your dad went the distance to become that better person like mine did, you owe it to yourself to let him in. You absolutely won't regret it. My dad's love has made me the complete person I was always supposed to be. God bless all the wonderful fathers in this world. You don't get enough credit for what you do for us.

Our relationship the last few years he was around was wonderful, we were so close and had amazing talks about life, vacationing together in the summer & never missed a weekly visit. When he was dying of brain cancer my brothers couldn't be bothered to smarten up and help out, I quit my job to take care of him full time so he wouldn't rott away in a hospital & instead stay at home... as hard as it was emotionally to see him wither away into a shell of his former self, it was the most enriching period of my life. It changed a lot of things in me to be his caregiver and accompany him to his death, I'd do it again without hesitation, screw careers, change is good anyways.

This allowed me to appreciate how he was during my childhood, being the sole captain of the ship I don't hold any short conings against him & actually understand the child rearing strategies he employed being alone with 3 boys. I could hold a lot of it against my mom for leaving like my brothers do but I chose not to, it would only create more negativity in my life and nobody needs that.
